reason: The septum fits the undivided heart chambers and establishes the separate right and left sides.
expectation: The partition should divide the heart into right and left sides, ready for valves.

effect: The septum divided the heart and revealed separate inlet and outlet valve slots.
reaction: The reversing arrows make the need for valves clear.
reason: The inlet valves match the ventricular inlets slot.
expectation: The inlet valves should fit between the upper chambers and ventricles.

effect: The inlet valves are installed and close against backward flow during ventricular contraction; the outlet slot remains.
reaction: The filling and squeezing frames clarify the valves’ role.
reason: The outlet valves match the remaining ventricular outlets slot.
expectation: The outlet valves should fit at the ventricular exits and help prevent backward flow.

effect: Both valve sets are fitted; the outlet valves limit backflow from the arteries between beats.
reaction: The contrast between ejection and the pause makes their role clear.
reason: The conducting tissue's pacemaker and pathways suggest it can coordinate the heart chambers.
expectation: The heart should gain electrical pathways that coordinate its beats.

effect: The heart now has conducting pathways that time atrial and ventricular contractions.
reaction: The timed wave makes the coordination clear.
reason: The pulmonary loop visibly connects the heart’s right and left sides through the lungs, matching one of the two required routes.
expectation: The pulmonary vessels should connect the heart to the lung capillary region and back.

effect: The pulmonary route now connects the right heart to the lungs and returns to the left atrium; the body route remains open.
reaction: The open connection makes the next step clear.
reason: The systemic vessel network supplies the separate route through body tissues.
expectation: The systemic vessels should connect the heart to the body tissues and back.

effect: The heart now connects to separate pulmonary and systemic vessel loops.
reaction: The two routes are assembled as expected.
reason: Blood is needed in the connected vessels to complete the circulation model.
expectation: The blood should fill the heart and vessel routes.

effect: Blood could not be added yet; the automatic combination first connected the heart’s own blood supply.
reaction: The distinction between blood in the chambers and the muscle’s coronary supply is useful.
reason: With the coronary vessels connected, blood remains the obvious ingredient for the circulation model.
expectation: Blood should enter the connected heart and vessel routes.

effect: Blood now fills the connected pulmonary and systemic routes, completing both goals; the arrows clarify the return to the heart after each route.
reaction: The completed two-loop schematic is satisfying and makes the overall route easy to follow.

mostWorthwhile.text: Connecting the coronary vessels was most worthwhile: it distinguishes the heart muscle’s own blood supply from blood passing through its chambers.

leastWorthwhile.text: Connecting the systemic network produced only a brief two-loop schematic, so that step felt less informative than the valve and coronary explanations.

surprise.text: I expected to add blood immediately, but the attempt instead revealed that the coronary vessels had to be connected first.

arbitrary.text: The requirement to connect coronary vessels before adding blood was not obvious beforehand, though the resulting explanation gave that connection a clear purpose.

continue.text: Yes. I would be interested in continuing because the coronary connection and the valve illustrations linked the assembled structures to their functions, even though some steps were predictable.
